Claude.notes: Turing's 1950 paper opens the module and cleanly generates the definitional question the concept section then unpacks. Behaviorism/cognitivism/embodied cognition are laid out as competing frames rather than a single answer, which is right for Advanced. Character consistency is the weak point — recurring figures (Turing, Spearman) anchor concepts but no protagonist carries across labs.
Claude.topIssue: The insight lands more by exposition than by the learner reaching it themselves — the closing frames tell the learner why the debate matters instead of letting the lab dialogue do that work.

Gemini.notes: Definitions of the Turing test and Spearman's g are directionally correct. The gloss on Spearman ('a general underlying factor that correlates across cognitive tasks') simplifies a debated psychometric construct — accurate as a first pass, but a learner could leave thinking g is settled science. Behaviorism/cognitivism/embodied cognition are cleanly separated.
Gemini.topIssue: The 'in a period of about two years, multiple systems passed [the Turing test] in most casual settings' claim is stronger than the primary literature supports — an operational Turing pass in the strict Turing 1950 sense has not been formally accepted by the AI research community.

Perplexity.notes: The 2026 framing is up to date and the module doesn't feel like a museum piece. Contemporary anchors (GPT-4-class systems, casual Turing-pass claims) tie a 1950 debate to current AI. Would benefit from citing at least one 2024–2026 benchmark (e.g. reasoning-oriented evals like ARC-AGI) alongside classical IQ constructs.
Perplexity.topIssue: The lab framing references 'GPT-4, whatever you like' — by 2026 the frontier has moved (Opus 5/Fable, GPT-5-class models); the module reads as slightly locked to 2023–2024 examples.

Claude.notes: Chalmers' easy/hard distinction is the spine, and the story of the Tucson consciousness conference lands the problem before it's named. Qualia and philosophical zombies are introduced with care — the module resists collapsing 'hard problem' into 'unsolved neuroscience,' which is the most common curricular misstep here.
Claude.topIssue: Story-to-concept ratio tilts concept-heavy even for Advanced; a stronger scene could bridge the transition from Chalmers-at-Tucson to the zombie thought experiment.

Gemini.notes: 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness' (JCS, 1995) and the Tucson conference series are cited correctly. The 'inaugural' Toward a Science of Consciousness label is slightly loose — the Tucson series' first conference was 1994 and Chalmers's paper post-dates it; a reader could infer the sequence wrong.
Gemini.topIssue: The philosophical-zombie argument is presented as if wide consensus finds it 'even conceivable' — several serious rebuttals (Dennett, Frankish's illusionism) get one-line mentions but not enough weight for the Advanced level.

Perplexity.notes: The hard problem is a durable debate; the module doesn't try to force novelty and that's fine. What it lacks is any 2024–2026 anchor — no reference to the Association for Mathematical Consciousness Science, no mention of the ongoing debate over LLM introspection reports as data (Anthropic's 2024 introspection work, Perez et al.), no nod to the neural-correlates-of-consciousness adversarial collaboration results.
Perplexity.topIssue: The quiz tests recognition of Chalmers's terminology more than application to a novel case; an Advanced learner should be asked to adjudicate a live 2025–2026 example rather than restate the framework.

Claude.notes: The BBS submission scene is a genuine hook — 27 hostile commentaries in the same issue is a story detail that pays dividends. Weak/Strong AI and the syntax/semantics distinction are cleanly separated. Searle carries across the module as a recurring figure, which lifts character consistency versus other modules.
Claude.topIssue: The lab prompts the learner to 'find at least one objection the argument cannot easily handle' — good task shape, but the module doesn't sequence the learner into a candidate objection first; strong learners will do fine, weaker Advanced learners may stall.

Gemini.notes: Citation is unusually precise for a lay-audience module: BBS vol. 3 no. 3, pp. 417–424, 1980 — verifiable. Intentionality, syntax, and semantics are defined with the correct philosophical weight. The Boden and Chalmers rebuttals are named at the right level of specificity.
Gemini.topIssue: The '11,000 citations as of 2024' figure is plausible but should be sourced to a specific database (Google Scholar) with an as-of date to avoid drift; otherwise the module ages into inaccuracy.

Perplexity.notes: The 1980 argument is timeless, but the module could do more to bring it into 2026 practice — mechanistic interpretability results (Anthropic's dictionary-learning work, Neel Nanda's circuits) genuinely stress the syntax/semantics line and would give Advanced learners a fresh application.
Perplexity.topIssue: The lab is executable but doesn't force the learner to confront a specific modern system's behavior against Searle's argument; without that, the discussion stays abstract.

Claude.notes: The Whanganui River personhood case is exactly the right narrative wedge — a legal moral-status decision that isn't about sentience prefigures the AI-rights debate cleanly. The four criteria are surfaced without collapsing into a single preferred answer, which respects the learner's own reasoning.
Claude.topIssue: Moral patient vs moral agent is a genuinely tricky distinction and the module defines it in one paragraph — the lab surfaces this but the concept section could earn the distinction with one more concrete example (e.g. a comatose adult).

Gemini.notes: Singer, Feinberg, and Kantian criteria are attributed correctly. Te Awa Tupua Act is real, but the module says 'September 2017' — the Act was passed 20 March 2017 in the NZ Parliament. Small but the kind of date slip that erodes trust when a learner checks the source.
Gemini.topIssue: The Whanganui date is off by roughly six months; either 'March 2017' or 'in 2017' would be correct. A verifiable case shouldn't sit next to a checkable date error.

Perplexity.notes: Whanganui 2017 is well-worn by 2026. The module misses easier and more current anchors: the 2024 debate over 'AI welfare' teams at frontier labs (Anthropic hired for model welfare in 2024), the Long/Sebo 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' paper (Nov 2024), and the ongoing regulatory language in the EU AI Act about non-human 'systems.'
Perplexity.topIssue: The Whanganui case study is nine years old and the module doesn't surface the 2024 model-welfare literature that has made this exact debate operational at frontier labs — an Advanced learner reading in 2026 will notice the gap.

Claude.notes: The 'mirror problem' framing is strong — Roose's Sydney transcript is exactly the kind of story that generates the exact question the concept section then answers ('are we perceiving the AI's states, our own projections, or something novel?'). The Weizenbaum/ELIZA callback anchors the point historically.
Claude.topIssue: The quiz leans on recall of Weizenbaum's biography rather than testing the mirror-problem judgment itself; the lab is where the learning actually happens but the assessment doesn't credit it.

Gemini.notes: ELIZA and Daniel Stern's attunement research are correctly cited. The 'summer of 2023' framing for Kevin Roose's Sydney transcript is wrong — Roose's column ran in the NYT on 16 February 2023. That's a checkable factual error on the module's single most vivid case.
Gemini.topIssue: The Sydney/Roose transcript is dated 'summer of 2023' — the NYT column was published 16 February 2023. A learner who verifies the module's headline example will lose trust in the rest of it.

Perplexity.notes: Sydney/Bing Chat is now three years old and no longer represents the frontier of AI self-description. The module doesn't reference the 2024 Character.AI teen-suicide lawsuit, the ongoing Replika regulatory battles, or Anthropic's 2024–2025 model welfare/introspection work — all of which are the current versions of the exact 'mirror problem' the module is trying to teach.
Perplexity.topIssue: The Sydney example predates the 2024 Character.AI lawsuit and the 2024–2025 wave of AI-companion regulation — cited in a 2026 module, it reads as historical rather than illustrative.

Claude.notes: The 'from academic thought experiment to institutional priority' arc is a real curriculum move — Bostrom 2014 → Omohundro drives → Russell's Human Compatible → MIRI → the Bletchley Declaration is the correct throughline for x-risk history, and the module builds it without breathlessness or dismissal.
Claude.topIssue: The paperclip maximizer is presented mostly as it lands from Bostrom; a stronger version would surface the sharper 2020s critique (Yann LeCun on instrumental convergence, Ng on 'the trolley problem for robots').

Gemini.notes: Bostrom's Superintelligence (2014), Omohundro's 'Basic AI Drives' (2008), Russell's Human Compatible (2019), and MIRI/Yudkowsky's founding (2000) are all correctly cited. 'August 2014' for Superintelligence is close enough — UK release was 3 July 2014 and US September 2014, so August is a defensible middle date.
Gemini.topIssue: The module says convergent instrumental goals 'emerge from optimization pressure itself' — that's the Omohundro/Bostrom claim, but it's contested (Shah, Krakovna) in a way an Advanced learner should be able to see; presenting it as settled overweights one side.

Perplexity.notes: The Bletchley Declaration (Nov 2023) is anchored, which is good, but by 2026 the follow-on institutional record is Seoul (May 2024), Paris (Feb 2025), EU AI Act general-purpose model rules (Aug 2025 phase), and the UK/US AISI network — none appear. The module reads as if the x-risk debate froze at Bletchley.
Perplexity.topIssue: The institutional-response section stops at Bletchley 2023; a 2026 module should cover Seoul 2024, Paris 2025, and the operational AISI network — otherwise the 'long view' looks short.
